rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs. The high final organic fraction reduces the risk of missing strongly retained compounds.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the crowded central cluster and the final pair. There is ample room below the 10-minute time penalty to optimize resolution afterward.
Test the low-temperature endpoint with the same gradient to map temperature-dependent selectivity. The current short elution window leaves room for increased retention without a time penalty.

Use a shallower gradient at the best temperature to test whether the two remaining critical pairs separate. The last peak at 7.23 minutes leaves room to increase gradient time while targeting elution near 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction to bring the elution window earlier while slightly reducing the gradient slope. This may lift the remaining critical pair above R = 1.5 without pushing the last peak past 10 minutes.
Lengthen the gradient by one step to improve the sole unresolved pair. The previous last peak at 8.99 minutes provides enough headroom to target full resolution while remaining below 10 minutes.

Injection 6 reached the maximum CRF; now seek a shorter fully resolved separation. Raise the starting organic fraction one step to advance elution, using the critical pair’s resolution margin as headroom.
Slightly flatten the gradient to recover resolution in the sole critical pair while retaining the earlier elution gained from phi0 = 0.20. Injection 6 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Raise temperature one step from the shortest fully resolved method to test whether elution can be accelerated while retaining R ≥ 1.5. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates the temperature effect on the critical pair.

Return to 25 C and raise the starting organic fraction to advance elution. Lower the final fraction to provide a shallower gradient that may preserve the critical central separation despite the higher start.
Test a 5 C increase on the latest fully resolved gradient to shorten retention. Its wider early-pair spacing at 25 C may tolerate the temperature shift better than injection 8 did.

Test a larger temperature shift on this shallow gradient to move beyond the late-pair convergence at 30 C and seek a faster fully resolved elution pattern. Retain injection 10 as the shortest confirmed maximum-score method.

Probe higher-temperature selectivity with the shallow gradient to see whether the central cluster opens after its order changes. This explores a faster separation while preserving injection 10 as the shortest confirmed fully resolved method.

Return to the successful low temperature and test a higher starting fraction with a substantially shallower gradient. This seeks earlier elution while compensating for the loss of central-pair resolution seen when the starting fraction alone was raised.

Test a faster, higher-organic-start regime that may separate the central pair on the opposite side of its elution-order crossover. The high final organic fraction limits the risk of retaining the late compounds beyond the acquisition window.
Shorten the gradient one step from the new fastest fully resolved method. This tests whether the late critical pair can retain R ≥ 1.5 while bringing the last peak earlier than 4.50 minutes.
Shorten the gradient another grid step to locate the resolution boundary. Injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method if either critical pair falls below R = 1.5.

Restore the successful 10-minute gradient and raise the starting organic fraction one step to accelerate elution through a different adjustment. This tests whether the central and late critical pairs retain full resolution at a higher starting strength.

Return to the fastest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature by 5 C to test a shorter separation. This isolates temperature selectivity after increasing the starting organic fraction caused central-pair overlap.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic fraction separates the central pair beyond its apparent convergence while shortening retention. Monitor the early pair for compression, keeping injection 16 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test whether a larger temperature shift reopens the central pair beyond the convergence seen at 30 C, enabling a faster fully resolved separation. Injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed method with CRF = 1.
Return to 25 C and test a lower starting fraction with a steeper gradient to rebalance the central separations in a short run. Injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score fallback.

Flatten the gradient at phi0 = 0.40 to recover the central-pair resolution lost in injection 18 while retaining its early elution advantage. This targets a fully resolved alternative near the speed of injection 16.

Test a smaller slope increase than the unsuccessful 8-minute gradient by raising phi1 one step from injection 16. This probes the fastest fully resolved boundary while retaining injection 16 as the confirmed maximum-score fallback.

Preserve injection 16’s successful gradient slope while shortening the programmed gradient to 4 minutes. Its outlet endpoint at 4.65 minutes follows the previously observed last peak at 4.14 minutes, so this should retain full resolution and CRF = 1.
